% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{center}\textbf{\large Abstract}\end{center}
\vspace{-0.4em}
\begin{quote}
Crop-type maps of Punjab's small farms could support food-security and water planning, but there are
no public field labels to train or test them on. A common workaround is to label fields from the
satellite time series itself, which risks an evaluation that only measures agreement with that
labelling. We sampled \NFields{} fields at random in a 10\,km square near Lahore, built 5-day
Sentinel-2 index series for each, and labelled the winter (Rabi 2026) crop: training fields from
clusters of their NDVI curves, and a separate blind test set from true-colour images only. Five
classifiers on two feature sets were compared with leave-one-strip-out spatial cross-validation, and
the chosen model, logistic regression on \NFeatB{} hand-made features, was evaluated once on the blind
test set. Spatial cross-validation gave \CVAcc{} accuracy; the blind test gave \TestAcc{}
(\TestCorrect/\NTest, $\pm$\TestMargin{} points) against a \BaselineTest{} majority baseline.
When training labels are derived from the same curves the model learns from, cross-validation
overstates accuracy, and an independently labelled test set is needed to measure by how much.
\end{quote}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}

Pakistani Punjab farms on a rice--wheat rotation: rice in the summer (Kharif) season, wheat and other
crops in the winter (Rabi) season. Knowing which crop grows where, field by field, is the starting
point for estimating harvests, planning irrigation water and tracking how land use changes. Free
Sentinel-2 imagery \cite{drusch2012sentinel2}, with a new image every five days at 10\,m resolution,
makes such maps possible in principle.

Two things make them hard to build and harder to trust. First, the fields are small: in our sample the
median field is about one acre, only a few dozen 10\,m pixels. Second, there are no public field-level
crop labels for the region, so labels must be made by hand, usually by looking at the same imagery the
model will learn from. A model trained and cross-validated on labels drawn from its own input curves
can score very well while learning little beyond the labelling rule.

This report measures that effect on a small, carefully controlled dataset. Our claim is that a simple
model on hand-made time-series features separates the main Rabi classes well, but that cross-validation
on curve-derived labels overstates its accuracy, and only an independently labelled blind test shows
by how much. The contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
  \item a labelled set of \NFields{} randomly sampled fields with field outlines, label provenance and a
        blind test protocol;
  \item a comparison of five classifiers and two feature sets under spatial cross-validation, with
        model selection fixed before the test set was opened;
  \item a measurement of the gap between curve-label cross-validation and the blind test, with an
        analysis of every test error.
\end{itemize}

We use Sentinel-2 surface reflectance \cite{drusch2012sentinel2} and standard vegetation indices,
NDVI above all \cite{tucker1979ndvi}. Our training labels follow the idea of
\citet{wang2019croptype}, who mapped crop types without field-level labels by clustering satellite
time series and naming the clusters. They validated against an independent official crop map; we have
no such map, so we created a blind test set labelled from a different source (true-colour imagery) and
treat the gap between the two evaluations as the main result. Neighbouring fields share soil, water,
sowing dates and weather, so randomly split cross-validation tends to be optimistic for spatial data;
block cross-validation that holds out whole areas is the recommended alternative
\cite{roberts2017cv}, and ignoring spatial structure can turn a seemingly useful map model into one
with almost no predictive power \cite{ploton2020spatial}. We use spatial blocks throughout.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Data}


\paragraph{Study area and imagery.} The study area is a 10\,$\times$\,10\,km square centred at
\CentreLat\,N, \CentreLon\,E, near Raiwind, south-west of Lahore, inside Sentinel-2 tile 43RDQ
(Figure~\ref{fig:area}). We used Level-2A surface reflectance from Microsoft Planetary Computer
\cite{planetarycomputer2022}, reading only the image blocks that cover the fields, from \FirstDate{} to
\LastDate{} (\NScenes{} dates with at least one usable field observation).

\paragraph{Pre-processing.} Digital numbers were converted to reflectance as
$(\mathrm{DN}-1000)/10000$, the offset used since processing baseline 04.00. Clouds and shadows were
taken from the Scene Classification Layer and grown by 2 pixels (20\,m), and a field was kept on a
date only if at least 80\% of its pixels were clear. Field outlines were shrunk by 5\,m so that only
pixels inside the field were used, and the 20\,m bands were resampled to 10\,m. Two further checks
flag observations the cloud mask misses: a scene-level haze flag (the median blue minus red reflectance
of dense fields, NDVI\,$>$\,0.5, above 0.006) and a dip flag (a value more than 0.1 below both
neighbouring observations, each within 20 days). Of \NObs{} field observations, \NFlagged{} were
flagged and left out of the series.

\paragraph{Indices and series.} For every field and date we took the median over the field's pixels of
five indices: NDVI (greenness), NDWI (open water), NDMI (moisture, from short-wave infrared), EVI
(greenness that saturates less in dense crops) and NDRE (red-edge chlorophyll). Each field's
observations were linearly interpolated onto a regular 5-day grid starting 1 September 2025; gaps longer
than 30 days were left empty rather than bridged. Smoothing was tested by holding out observations and
predicting them, and no smoothing gave the lowest error, so none was applied. Two gaps are shared by
almost every field: early December to late January (winter fog and smog) and mid-July to mid-August
(monsoon cloud).


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Labels}

\paragraph{Sampling and outlines.} One point was placed at random in each 1\,km cell of the square
(seed 2026), so that the sample was not biased towards large or easy fields. A field outline was grown
from each point over neighbouring pixels whose monthly NDVI through the whole year matched the point's;
the similarity threshold (0.08) was calibrated by overlap with three hand-drawn fields. Thirteen
outlines that the procedure flagged as doubtful were reviewed against high-resolution imagery: four were
kept and nine were labelled non\_crop (villages, roads, canal banks).

\paragraph{Blind test set.} Six points per strip, 30 in all, were set aside before any labelling and
labelled from true-colour images only, never from NDVI. Being exact about who labelled what: of the
30, \NClaudeLabels{} were labelled by an AI model (Claude) from true-colour image chips at the author's
request, and \NNotFullyBlind{} of those had had their NDVI profile seen during the outline review, so
they are not fully blind. The other \NTestFromReview{} were labelled non\_crop during the outline
review, which used both imagery and NDVI.

\paragraph{Training labels.} The training fields were clustered by k-means on their NDVI series, with
the test fields excluded so their labels could not leak in; the number of clusters (six) was chosen by
silhouette score. Each cluster was named from its median curve, and fields that fitted their cluster
poorly were read one by one. This gave \NCurveLabels{} curve-derived labels; the remaining training
fields carry non\_crop labels from the outline review.

\paragraph{Classes.} Several Rabi classes have only one or two training examples, too few to learn
from, so they were merged into three classes by what they mean on the ground (Table~\ref{tab:data}):
wheat; other\_crop (other winter crops, short winter crops, sugarcane, orchards); and not\_cropped
(non-crop land and fallow). Fields labelled unknown were left out, which leaves \NTrain{} training and
\NTest{} test fields. Figure~\ref{fig:profiles} shows why the classes are separable: wheat greens up over
December and January and is harvested in late March and April, other crops stay green into May, and the
median NDVI of non-cropped land stays below about 0.2 all year.


\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/profiles.pdf}
  \caption{Median NDVI (lines) and interquartile range (bands) of the training fields in each class.
  The shaded window, October to May, is the period the features are taken from. Wheat and other crops
  are both green in February; they separate in April, when wheat is harvested. The gaps are the
  winter fog and monsoon periods.}

\end{figure}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Methods}

\paragraph{Features.} Set A is the full curve: every index on every 5-day date from 1 October 2025 to
31 May 2026, after dropping dates that are missing for more than half the fields. That leaves
\NFeatA{} features (5 indices $\times$ \NDatesA{} dates), more than the \NTrain{} training fields.
Set B has \NFeatB{} hand-made features: monthly mean NDVI from October to May (8); the Rabi peak NDVI
and its date; the number of days with NDVI above 0.5; the minimum NDVI at sowing time; mean NDMI and
NDWI in March; peak EVI; and mean NDRE in February. Any remaining missing value is replaced by the
median of the training folds only.

\paragraph{Models.} All models come from scikit-learn \cite{pedregosa2011sklearn}: a majority-class
baseline; multinomial logistic regression with an L2 penalty; an SVM with an RBF kernel; a random
forest \cite{breiman2001rf} of 500 trees; and gradient boosting \cite{friedman2001gbm} with 200 rounds
of depth-2 trees, learning rate 0.05. Logistic regression and the SVM use standardised features. To
stop the 44 wheat fields from dominating, every model weights classes inversely to their frequency.
For logistic regression with weights $W$ and class weights $s_y$, training minimises
\begin{equation}
  \frac{1}{2}\lVert W \rVert^2 \;-\; C \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_{y_i} \log p(y_i \mid x_i; W),
\end{equation}
where a small $C$ means strong regularisation. $C$ was tuned over $\{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10\}$ for logistic
regression and $\{0.1, 1, 10, 100\}$ for the SVM.

\paragraph{Evaluation.} The main estimate is leave-one-strip-out cross-validation: each of the five
strips is predicted by a model trained on the other four. $C$ is chosen inside each training set by the
same leave-one-strip-out scheme (nested cross-validation), so the held-out strip never influences any
choice. For comparison only, we also report stratified random 5-fold cross-validation, repeated five
times; the difference between the two measures how much neighbouring fields help
\cite{roberts2017cv}. Among the eight trained combinations (four models, two feature sets), we chose the simplest one
within one standard error of the best spatial score (the one-standard-error rule
\cite{hastie2009esl}), preferring fewer features first and then the simpler model. This rule was
fixed before the blind test set was opened, and the test set was then used exactly once.

\paragraph{Metrics.} We report accuracy, the recall of each class, and balanced accuracy, the mean
recall over the $K=3$ classes,
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{BA} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\#\{i : y_i = k,\ \hat y_i = k\}}{\#\{i : y_i = k\}},
\end{equation}
which counts each class equally. For an accuracy $p$ on $n$ fields, the approximate 95\% interval is
$p \pm 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

\paragraph{Model comparison.} Table~\ref{tab:models} gives the balanced accuracy of every combination.
The best spatial score was \TopBal, with a standard error of \SE, and \NNearTop{} of the eight trained
combinations fell within one standard error of it. The rule therefore chose the simplest: set
\ChosenSet{} with \ChosenModel{} ($C = \ChosenC$). In spatial cross-validation this model reached
\CVAcc{} accuracy (\CVCorrect/\NTrain) and \CVBal{} balanced accuracy, against \BaselineTrain{} accuracy
for always predicting wheat. Random cross-validation gave \RandomBal{} balanced accuracy, no higher than
the spatial estimate.

\paragraph{Blind test.} On the \NTest{} blind test fields the model reached \TestAcc{} accuracy
(\TestCorrect/\NTest, $\pm$\TestMargin{} points, so the true value could be as low as \TestLow) and
\TestBal{} balanced accuracy, against \BaselineTest{} (\TestBaselineCorrect/\NTest) for always
predicting wheat (Table~\ref{tab:test}, Figure~\ref{fig:confusion}). All wheat fields were classified
correctly; the three errors were two not\_cropped fields predicted as other\_crop and one other\_crop
field predicted as wheat. On the test labels marked high-confidence, the model was correct on
\NHighCorrect{} of \NHigh.

\paragraph{Label confidence.} Training only on the \NTrainHighMed{} high- and medium-confidence labels
lowered spatial cross-validation accuracy to \ConfCleanAcc{} (balanced \ConfCleanBal), from
\ConfAllAcc{} (balanced \ConfAllBal) with all \NTrain{} labels.

\paragraph{Feature weights.} April NDVI carries the largest weights (Figure~\ref{fig:weights}): strongly
negative for wheat and strongly positive for other\_crop. Moisture and water in March (NDMI, NDWI) and
the number of days above NDVI 0.5 add to the same separation, while low peak NDVI and EVI point to
not\_cropped.

\section{Error analysis}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/errors.pdf}
  \caption{The three blind-test errors (black) with the median training curves of their labelled class
  (solid) and predicted class (dashed).}
  \label{fig:errors}
\end{figure}

Each blind-test error is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:errors} against the median curves of its labelled and
predicted classes.

\paragraph{\field{g0000}: canal-bank trees.} The outline covers a line of trees along a canal, labelled
non\_crop. Its mean NDVI from January to April is \WinterGzero, while no not\_cropped training field
exceeds \WinterNonCropMax. The training set contains no green non-crop land at all, and the only
fields in it that stay green all winter are orchards and sugarcane, labelled other\_crop. Given that data, other\_crop is the
reasonable answer; the error comes from a gap in the training set, not from the model.

\paragraph{\field{g0202}: point and outline disagree.} The sample point lies on a road verge, which is
what the label describes. The outline grown from it, however, covers the green patch beside the verge
(mean January--April NDVI \WinterGtwo), and the features describe the outline. The model may well be
right about the outline; the error lies in the boundary step, where a label for a point was attached
to an area it does not describe.

\paragraph{\field{g0600}: an early winter crop.} This field is green from December, is harvested in
early March, about a month before wheat, and then grows a second crop in April and May. The model
called it wheat. The only spatial cross-validation error (\field{g0608}, a short winter crop) is the
same confusion: a crop that is green through the winter and gone by April looks like wheat to features
that mostly ask whether a field is green in winter and bare in April. This is a genuine model
weakness; a feature for the timing of the harvest, such as the date NDVI falls below half its peak,
would be a natural addition.


% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Discussion and limitations}

\paragraph{The gap is the result.} Accuracy fell by \GapAcc{} points from spatial cross-validation to
the blind test, and balanced accuracy by \GapBal{} points. The training labels were made by clustering
the same NDVI curves the models learn from, so cross-validation largely measured how well a model can
recover that clustering, which seven of eight combinations did almost perfectly. The blind test labels
came from a different source, true-colour images, and so measure agreement with an independent reading
of the ground. The two errors on not\_cropped fields show the gap concretely: one comes from a kind of
land the curve-based training set never contained, the other from a mismatch between a point label and
its outline.

\paragraph{Simple was enough.} With \NFeatA{} features for \NTrain{} fields, set A gives a model enough
freedom to memorise the training set, yet regularised models on it scored no better than those on the
\NFeatB{} hand-made features of set B. A few moments in the season, the January green-up, the March
peak and the April harvest, carry nearly all the information, and the hand-made features encode them
directly. Because the differences between the top models were smaller than the noise in the estimate,
the one-standard-error rule picked the simplest, which is also the easiest to interpret.

\paragraph{No neighbour effect could be measured.} Random cross-validation was not more optimistic than
spatial cross-validation here. With scores near the ceiling there is little room for a gap, so this
result neither confirms nor rules out spatial dependence among these fields.

\paragraph{Limitations.} We group them by the kind of validity they threaten.
\emph{Internal:} the training labels are circular, as discussed above.
\emph{Construct:} the test labels are an AI model's reading of true-colour images rather than field
visits, \NNotFullyBlind{} of them were made after the field's NDVI had been seen, \NTestFromReview{}
come from an outline review that used NDVI, and a point label does not always describe its outline.
\emph{External:} one 10\,km square and one season, so the results may not hold where crop calendars or
field sizes differ.
\emph{Statistical:} with \NTest{} test fields, one field is about 4 points, and the 95\% interval is
$\pm$\TestMargin{} points; differences of a few fields between models cannot be resolved.
Finally, the test set has now been used: any change made in response to these errors must be judged on
new blind fields, not on these.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion and future work}

A logistic regression on \NFeatB{} hand-made Sentinel-2 features separated wheat, other crops and
non-cropped land near Lahore with \TestAcc{} accuracy on a blind test set, against \BaselineTest{} for
the majority class, while cross-validation on curve-derived labels had suggested \CVAcc. The
difference is the price of labelling from the model's own input, and only an independent test set
revealed it. Next steps are to add green non-crop land and early winter crops to the training set, to
check labels in the field, to fill the winter and monsoon gaps with Sentinel-1 radar, which sees
through cloud, and to test the model in a second district.
